Header: Cassava Brown Streak Virus Kinyarwanda: Kabore

Prevention: Plant virus-free' planting material from inspected fields (RAB and seed multipliers)
Do not move cassava cuttings from affected areas to new fields.
Uproot and bury all cassava volunteer plants
Dry all stems after harvesting and use them as fire wood or stakes.
Do not leave them on the farm
Remove weeds to discourage habitat for the vectors
Monitoring: Look for interveinal chlorosis and chlorotic blotches on lower/old leaves 3 months after planting, once a month until harvesting time.
Check for dark brown streaks on upper, young green stem 6 months after planting.
In severe cases there may be leaf drying and shoot die-back
Observe brown necrosis and hard rot inside the tuber when you cut it at 10 months after planting.
It often causes reduction in root size, root constriction and malformation.
Take action when one infected plant is observed
Direct Control: Remove diseased plants, dry them and use them as fire wood or stakes for climbing crops like beans.
Early harvesting at least 10 to 12 months after planting to reduce yield losses.
Restrictions: There is no chemical control against viruses
Use of pesticides to control vectors (whiteflies) on cassava is not pratical: insecticides can kill natural enemies such as
Apoanagyrus lopezi released before 1990 to control cassava mealybugs and
Typhlodromalus aripo (natural enemy of cassava green mites).
Protection equipments (PPE) and follow the instructions on the product label.
